summaries.example: Imagine the word “cat.” By itself, it can point to cats in general. In “The calico cat is sleeping,” the word “calico” makes the group smaller. Lambert studied how words can point to things differently depending on the words and situation around them.
summaries.summary: Lambert of Auxerre was a medieval logician associated with a major textbook called the Summa Lamberti. The book belongs to a movement called terminist logic, which examined words and their properties in sentences and arguments. Lambert explained how a term can stand for things, how added words or a situation can narrow its range, and how language can express possibility and connections. His identity is uncertain: some scholars connect him with Auxerre, others with Lagny or Ligny-le-Châtel. The book’s date is also given as a range, roughly the middle of the thirteenth century. Even with these uncertainties, the work became widely known and helped teach logic.
key_ideas: Lambert was a thirteenth-century teacher and logician, but scholars are not completely sure which Lambert he was.
His Summa Lamberti was an important textbook in medieval logic.
He studied how words work in sentences, including how their meaning can change with context.
He discussed restriction, different kinds of possibility, and relations between words or ideas.
The book was known by the end of the thirteenth century and was used for teaching at the Sorbonne.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lambert shows that people in the Middle Ages were studying language in a very detailed way. His questions are still useful: What does a word refer to? Does context change it? How can we tell whether an argument is sound? Studying his book also teaches us to be careful when evidence about the past is incomplete.

important_terms.definition: A careful way of thinking about whether an argument makes sense and whether its conclusion follows from its starting points.
A medieval approach to logic that studied words, what they stand for, and how they work in sentences.
Lambert’s large textbook about logic, written in Latin in the thirteenth century.
The way a word stands for something in a sentence or discussion.
A change that makes a word stand for fewer things.

summaries.example: Consider “The king is coming.” The word “king” could refer to many kings in general, but in a particular country and conversation it may refer to that country’s current king. Lambert calls this kind of narrowing use-based restriction. By contrast, “calico cat” narrows “cat” through an added expression. The distinction shows how both sentence structure and context affect what a term stands for.
summaries.summary: Lambert of Auxerre is the conventional title for a thirteenth-century French logician whose authorship of the Summa Lamberti is not securely identified. The treatise is a comprehensive textbook belonging to terminist logic, a medieval development centered on terms, their semantic and grammatical properties, and their combination into propositions and syllogistic arguments. Its dating is usually placed around 1250–1260, although scholars propose somewhat different ranges. The entry emphasizes Lambert’s treatment of supposition and appellation. He separates several ordinary and technical uses of these terms and analyzes how a term stands for objects or instances in a proposition. He also distinguishes restriction produced by an added term from restriction supplied by context, surveys basic alethic modalities, and treats relation as a linguistic device for recalling something previously introduced. The Summa was used in teaching and was known widely by the late thirteenth century, but claims about particular later influences must be made cautiously.
key_ideas: The Summa Lamberti is one of four major textbooks representing the mature development of terminist logic in the period roughly 1175–1270.
The author’s identity remains unsettled. Manuscripts and later scholarship connect him variously with Auxerre, Lagny, and Ligny-le-Châtel.
Lambert distinguishes several uses of “supposition” and “appellation,” reserving special senses for logical analysis of terms.
His account recognizes both natural restriction and restriction governed by conversational or situational use.
His treatment of modality is largely traditional, but he gives special attention to some rules for contingent propositions.
The work was widely known by the late thirteenth century, though the exact paths of its influence remain partly uncertain.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lambert’s work connects philosophy of language with practical reasoning. It shows that medieval logicians were not merely memorizing rules: they analyzed reference, context, ambiguity, and the logical force of modal claims. It also provides a lesson in historical method. Manuscripts preserve evidence, but that evidence may support more than one reconstruction, so responsible scholarship sometimes preserves uncertainty rather than forcing a final identification.

important_terms.definition: A thirteenth-century form of medieval logic focused on terms, their properties, and how terms combine into propositions and arguments.
In Lambert’s main logical sense, the way a term stands for itself, its referent, or one or more things falling under what it signifies within a proposition.
A related but distinct notion concerning how a term is taken for an actually existing suppositum or supposita in logical use.
A reduction in the range of things for which a term stands, caused either by an added expression or by the context of use.
An increase in the range of things for which a term stands; it is discussed alongside restriction in terminist theories.
A statement’s mode of being true or false, such as necessity, impossibility, possibility, or contingency.
A linguistic or syntactic way of recalling something introduced earlier, distinct from relation as a mutual connection between things.
Lambert’s Latin logic textbook, probably composed and edited during the middle decades of the thirteenth century.

Does “The king is coming” depend on shared context to identify its subject?

What is gained by distinguishing possibility from contingency?
Can a theory of language remain consistent if one term has several technical uses?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “The team is ready.” Which team? In a conversation about your school, listeners may understand “the team” to mean the school team. The surrounding situation limits the word’s range. If the student says, “The soccer team is ready,” the added word “soccer” limits it through the expression itself. Lambert’s theory of restriction helps separate these two ways of narrowing what a term stands for.
summaries.summary: Lambert of Auxerre refers to a medieval logician whose name and biography are still debated. His Summa Lamberti was a substantial Latin textbook written during the period when terminist logic was developing. Unlike a simple list of rules, this kind of logic examines terms: what they signify, what they stand for in a sentence, and how they combine into arguments. Lambert’s most distinctive discussions concern supposition and appellation. He separates several meanings of these words and focuses on their specifically logical roles. He also explains how a term can be restricted by an added description, such as “calico” narrowing “cat,” or by the context, such as “the king” being understood as the ruler relevant to a conversation. The book covers basic modal ideas—necessity, impossibility, possibility, and contingency—as well as relations in language. Its date is uncertain within a middle-thirteenth-century range, and scholars disagree about its author’s exact identity. Still, the work was widely circulated and used in education.
key_ideas: Lambert wrote the Summa Lamberti, one of the major logic textbooks of the later thirteenth-century terminist movement.
We cannot be certain whether the author was Lambert of Auxerre, Lambert of Lagny, or Lambert of Ligny-le-Châtel; the entry therefore usually says simply “Lambert.”
Lambert explains that “supposition” has several uses, but the logical use concerns what a term stands for in a proposition.
He identifies two kinds of restriction: one caused by added language and another caused by context.
His discussions of modality mostly follow familiar Aristotelian themes, while his treatment of contingent statements includes a more detailed point.
The textbook circulated widely and was used at the Sorbonne, although the extent of its influence on individual later thinkers is debated.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lambert’s analysis helps explain why understanding a sentence involves more than knowing dictionary definitions. Grammar, context, and logical role all matter. His case also shows how philosophy and history work together: interpreting an old theory requires examining manuscripts, comparing related thinkers, and distinguishing what the evidence establishes from what it merely suggests.

important_terms.definition: The study of good reasoning, including how statements fit together to support conclusions.
A medieval style of logic that focused on terms, what they stand for, and how they function in statements.
A term’s role in standing for one thing, several things, or something described by the term within a proposition.
A technical idea about taking a term to refer to actual things that fall under it.
Making a term stand for a smaller group, either by adding words or through the situation in which it is used.
Making a term stand for a wider group than it normally would.
The status of a statement as necessary, impossible, possible, contingent, true, or false.
A connection in language that brings an earlier thing or expression back to mind.
